screens.title: Getting Started with Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Today we begin by preparing your development environment so you can move from zero to a working Unity project. First, you will install Unity Hub, sign in with a Unity ID, and use the Hub to add a stable Unity Editor version. Then you will create a new project from the 3D Core template, inspect the Editor layout, and add your first 3D object. These setup steps are foundational: a correct Editor install plus consistent project organization prevents version mismatch issues and saves time when you iterate or collaborate. For example, selecting a Long Term Support Editor version and including Visual Studio ensures stable C# scripting and debugging tools later. We'll also show the five core windows you will use constantly: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector. By the end of this lesson you will have a named project folder, a saved scene named MainScene, and a cube you can move, rotate, and scale. If you skip module or build support modules now, you may hit missing-platform errors later. Take this setup slowly and double-check options during installation; it pays off when you start building. What small habit will you adopt now to keep your projects organized?

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Getting Started
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Getting Started with Unity

Install Unity Hub and the Unity Editor, create a 3D Core project, and learn the key Editor windows so you can build and save your first 3D scene.

In this lesson
Set up Hub and Editor, create a 3D project, explore the Editor, and add a cube you can manipulate.
Why this matters
A correct install and stable Editor version prevent future build and scripting issues, and consistent folders help collaboration.
Explore Key Topics
A quick map of what you'll practice
Install
Unity Hub, Editor, and recommended modules like Visual Studio.
Create
New project from the 3D Core template, choose a clear name and location.
Build
Add a cube, use transform tools, save a MainScene to preserve work.
Concept map
setup → project → editor
Unity Hub
Installs and manages Editors and projects
Editor
Design, script, and test your game
Project
A folder containing assets, scenes, and settings

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives describe concrete skills you will gain while setting up Unity and creating your first 3D project. First, you will install Unity Hub and a recommended Editor version so your environment matches common project requirements. Practically, this means selecting build support modules and Visual Studio during installation. Second, you will create a new project using the 3D Core template and give it a clear name and folder location so that your assets stay organized. Third, you will identify the Editor’s primary windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and understand each window’s role in development. Finally, you will manipulate a 3D object using the Move, Rotate, and Scale tools and change Transform values directly in the Inspector, then save your scene and project. Each objective includes a short description that ties the skill to a real task, and a verified competency milestone you can use to confirm you completed it. These steps reduce friction on future tasks and form a reliable baseline for every project you create.

screens.title: Objectives — What success looks like
screens.narratorSegment: Measure your setup by small, verifiable milestones. You have installed Unity Hub and logged in with a Unity ID when the Hub shows your account and offers Editor installs. You have installed an Editor with recommended modules when the Editor opens without missing build support warnings and Visual Studio launches for script editing. You’ve created a named 3D Core project when the Hub lists that project and opening it launches the Editor with a default scene. You can identify the five core Editor windows: Scene for constructing the world, Game for previewing camera output, Hierarchy for the scene’s GameObjects, Project for assets, and Inspector for component configuration. These are small, observable actions you can use to confirm competence and to avoid common mistakes like leaving assets unorganized or not saving your work.

screens.title: Install Unity Hub and sign in
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Unity Hub is the first practical step and it functions like mission control for your Unity installations. Unity Hub centralizes Editor versions and project management so you can install multiple Editor builds side-by-side. Begin by downloading the Hub installer from the provided source and follow the installer steps. When you first open Hub you'll be prompted to sign in with a Unity ID — creating one is a short, free process and it links your license and services. A common practical decision is to enable automatic updates or to pin an Editor version; for reproducibility, choose a stable recommended release or the Long Term Support version. After signing in, confirm Hub shows your account and offers the Editor installs page. A common misconception is that you must use the newest Editor right away; in many cases a stable LTS version reduces chance of breaking changes while you learn. Example: choose LTS if collaborating with teammates who use that version. Now consider build modules: include Visual Studio for scripting and your platform build support to prevent later build-time errors. This careful installation reduces interruptions when you begin scripting and building player targets.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Install Unity Hub
Install flow
1
Download and run the Hub installer
Follow installer prompts and open Unity Hub when finished.
2
Sign in with a Unity ID
Create a Unity ID if needed; sign in to manage licenses and services.
3
Install an Editor
Choose a stable LTS or recommended build; add Visual Studio and platform modules.
Key Takeaway

Install Hub first, sign-in, then add an Editor with the modules you’ll need for development and builds.

Practical tips & example
  • Choose LTS when starting a learning or production project to minimize breaking updates.
  • Include Visual Studio Community so you can edit and debug C# scripts immediately.
  • Select your platform build support now if you know the target, such as Windows or mobile, to avoid reinstall later.
Common mistake
Skipping build modules or Visual Studio during Editor install leads to missing tools and additional reinstallation steps later.

screens.title: Install Editor and choose modules
screens.narratorSegment: After Hub is ready, you install a Unity Editor build and choose supporting modules. The Editor is the tool you will use to author scenes, attach scripts, and build players. When the Hub lists available Editor versions, consider the Long Term Support release because it prioritizes stability—useful when you move from tutorials to projects. During install, the Hub offers optional modules. For 3D development, include platform build support for your operating system and any target platforms you intend to test, such as Android or iOS, to avoid re-running the installer later. Also add Visual Studio Community so your code editing and debugging work smoothly. A concrete example: if you plan to test on Windows and Android, include Windows Build Support and Android Build Support during installation. A common misconception is that these modules can be skipped and added later without consequence; while you can add them later, doing so mid-project may interrupt your workflow and require a reinstall. Once installation completes, launch the Editor to verify that Visual Studio links and the Editor open without missing-module warnings. Install Editor and choose modules means install platform build support and visual studio during editor setup to enable building and scripting without later interruptions.. In practical terms, select an editor version and required modules for 3d development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Editor & Modules
Choose Editor version

Prefer a stable or LTS release. Stability reduces risk of breaking API changes while you learn or collaborate.

Recommended module
Visual Studio Community — essential for C# editing and debugging.
Platform support
Add your target builds like Windows, Android, or iOS to avoid later reinstalls.
Example:
If you will test on Windows and Android, choose Windows Build Support and Android Build Support during the Editor install. This prevents missing SDK errors when building your player later.
Installer checklist

screens.title: Create a new 3D Core project
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new project is straightforward but important for long-term organization. In Unity Hub, click New Project and choose the 3D Core template. This template gives a clean starting scene with a camera and a directional light without unnecessary assets. Choose a meaningful project name such as MyFirst3DGame and select a dedicated location on your disk—preferably a Projects folder you keep for all Unity work. The folder location is critical: placing your project in a synced or shared folder can complicate locks and large asset syncing, so choose reliably accessible storage. When you click Create Project, Unity will open the Editor with the default layout and a new untitled scene. Immediately save the scene via File > Save Scene and name it MainScene. Saving early avoids losing work and establishes a predictable file structure. A common mistake is using cryptic or generic project names, which makes collaboration and version control harder. Naming and saving consistently is a small habit that pays off across a project’s lifetime. Create a new 3D Core project means pick a clear project name and dedicated folder, then save the initial scene as mainscene to anchor your project file structure.. In practical terms, name, locate, and initialize your first scene. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Create Project
Create steps
  1. Select New Project → 3D Core template.
  2. Enter a descriptive name, e.g., MyFirst3DGame.
  3. Choose a dedicated folder location—prefer a Projects directory.
  4. Click Create Project and wait for the Editor to open.
  5. Immediately save the scene as MainScene (File → Save Scene).
Key Takeaway

Name and save early. A saved MainScene and a clear project folder avoid later confusion.

Why location matters
Choosing a consistent Projects folder prevents fragmented files, simplifies backups, and reduces confusion when opening projects later.
Common mistake
Saving scenes to the wrong folder or leaving projects unnamed makes collaboration and version control harder.

screens.title: Unity Editor layout explained
screens.narratorSegment: The Unity Editor is composed of a few interdependent windows you will use constantly. First, the Scene View is your interactive workspace where you place and arrange objects, adjust lighting, and visually build the game world. Think of it as a 3D canvas. The Game View renders what the active camera sees and helps you evaluate gameplay and framing. The Hierarchy shows a nested list of all GameObjects in the open scene; parenting affects transforms so a child moves with its parent. The Project window is your asset browser where models, scripts, textures, and audio live; keeping it tidy with descriptive folders prevents clutter. Finally, the Inspector exposes the properties and components of the currently selected GameObject or asset so you can edit Transform values, add components, or attach scripts. A common misconception is that the Hierarchy and Project windows list the same things — they do not. Hierarchy lists instances in the scene, Project lists source assets on disk. Example: importing a model appears in Project, and dragging it into the Scene creates a GameObject visible in Hierarchy. Understanding these roles makes navigation and editing efficient.

keyIdea.text: Scene and Game handle visual work, Hierarchy lists scene instances, Project stores assets, and Inspector edits properties.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Editor Layout
Editor windows at a glance
Scene View
Interactive 3D workspace for arranging objects, lights, and level design.
Game View
Rendered output from the active camera — what players will see during play.
Hierarchy
Lists GameObjects in the scene; supports parent-child relationships and transforms.
Project
Asset browser showing files on disk, like models and scripts; keep folders tidy.
Inspector
When you select a GameObject or asset, the Inspector exposes its components and properties so you can edit transforms, add scripts, and change settings.
Misconception
The Project window does not show instances in the scene — it shows source assets on disk. Use Project to import, Hierarchy to place.

screens.title: Scene View navigation controls
screens.narratorSegment: Scene navigation is a small set of controls that dramatically speed up level design once you practice them. The basic actions are pan, zoom, orbit, fly, and focus. Pan by holding the middle mouse button and dragging; this moves the Scene camera laterally. Zoom with the mouse scroll wheel to get closer to or farther from targets. Orbit by holding the right mouse button and dragging to rotate the camera around a pivot point; combine this with W, A, S, D to 'fly' through the scene while the right mouse button is held for first-person style movement. Use Q and E for vertical strafing. A highly useful shortcut is pressing F when an object is selected to focus the Scene camera on that object — the camera will center and zoom appropriately. A common novice mistake is confusing Scene and Game camera controls; Scene navigation affects your editing viewpoint only and does not change the game camera unless you edit that camera object. Example: select a cube and press F to immediately center it, then use W and right mouse to move closer while orbiting to inspect its surface. Practicing these controls makes placement and alignment much faster.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Scene Navigation
Navigation actions
  • Pan: middle mouse drag — moves the camera laterally.
  • Zoom: scroll wheel — change distance to pivot.
  • Orbit: right mouse drag — rotate around pivot point.
  • Fly: hold right mouse and use W/A/S/D, Q/E for vertical movement.
  • Focus (F): centers and zooms the camera on the selected object for quick inspection.
Key Takeaway

Master F and right-mouse navigation to inspect objects quickly and align elements faster.

Practice drill
Select your cube, press F to focus, then hold right mouse and press W to fly toward it. Orbit to inspect all sides, then use middle mouse to pan across the scene.
Misconception
Moving the Scene camera does not move the game camera unless you explicitly move the Camera GameObject itself.

screens.title: Add objects and use transform tools
screens.narratorSegment: Adding GameObjects and manipulating their Transform component is one of the most frequent actions in Unity. To add your first object, right-click in the Hierarchy, choose 3D Object, and select Cube. The new Cube appears in the Scene View and as an entry in the Hierarchy. To move it, press W to activate the Move tool and drag the colored axes or use numeric values in the Transform component inside the Inspector. Press E for Rotate and R for Scale. A concrete example: place the Cube at position X:0, Y:1, Z:0 so it sits above the ground; rotate it 45 degrees on the Y axis to change its facing; scale it to 2 on the X axis to make it rectangular. A common beginner mistake is confusing which tool is active; if your object rotates when you intend to move it, switch to the Move tool with 'W'. Another tip is that you can type values directly into the Inspector for precise control. Practice both dragging handles and typing values so you can prototype quickly and then fine-tune numerically when precision is required.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Add & Transform
Create a Cube
Right-click in Hierarchy → 3D Object → Cube. The object appears in Scene and Hierarchy as an instance of an asset.
W — Move
E — Rotate
R — Scale
Type Transform values in the Inspector for precise placement. For example, set Position to 0,1,0 so the cube sits above the ground plane.
Example workflow
  1. Add Cube in Hierarchy.
  2. Press W and drag the green axis to move it up, or set Y to 1 in Inspector.
  3. Press E and rotate Y to 45 degrees for facing change.
  4. Press R and scale X to 2 to stretch along X axis.
Pro tip
Use Inspector for exact values and transform handles for quick adjustments; both are useful in different stages of iteration.

screens.title: Project Window organization
screens.narratorSegment: Good project organization from the start saves hours later. The Project window is where assets live on disk and clutter builds up quickly if you leave everything at root. Adopt a simple folder structure such as Assets/Art, Assets/Scripts, Assets/Prefabs, Assets/Audio. Use descriptive file and folder names so assets are discoverable; for example, name a hero model Hero_V1 rather than model1. Importing a model places it into Project, and dragging it into the Scene creates an instance in the Hierarchy. A common rookie mistake is leaving many imported assets uncategorized, which slows you and your team. A practical habit is to create folders before importing and move new items into correct folders immediately. Also save scenes frequently with meaningful names like MainScene or Level01. Example: after importing a package, move textures into Art/Textures and meshes into Art/Models. This small organizational discipline reduces merge conflicts and makes searching faster when projects grow. Project Window organization means create clear folders and naming patterns before importing assets; save scenes with descriptive names to avoid confusion.. In practical terms, keep assets tidy with folders and naming conventions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Project Organization
Suggested folder structure
  • Assets/Art — models, textures
  • Assets/Scripts — C# scripts and utilities
  • Assets/Prefabs — reusable GameObjects saved as prefabs
  • Assets/Audio — sound effects and music

fullNarratorScript:
Today we begin by preparing your development environment so you can move from zero to a working Unity project. First, you will install Unity Hub, sign in with a Unity ID, and use the Hub to add a stable Unity Editor version. Then you will create a new project from the 3D Core template, inspect the Editor layout, and add your first 3D object. These setup steps are foundational: a correct Editor install plus consistent project organization prevents version mismatch issues and saves time when you iterate or collaborate. For example, selecting a Long Term Support Editor version and including Visual Studio ensures stable C# scripting and debugging tools later. We'll also show the five core windows you will use constantly: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector. By the end of this lesson you will have a named project folder, a saved scene named MainScene, and a cube you can move, rotate, and scale. If you skip module or build support modules now, you may hit missing-platform errors later. Take this setup slowly and double-check options during installation; it pays off when you start building. What small habit will you adopt now to keep your projects organized?

These learning objectives describe concrete skills you will gain while setting up Unity and creating your first 3D project. First, you will install Unity Hub and a recommended Editor version so your environment matches common project requirements. Practically, this means selecting build support modules and Visual Studio during installation. Second, you will create a new project using the 3D Core template and give it a clear name and folder location so that your assets stay organized. Third, you will identify the Editor’s primary windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and understand each window’s role in development. Finally, you will manipulate a 3D object using the Move, Rotate, and Scale tools and change Transform values directly in the Inspector, then save your scene and project. Each objective includes a short description that ties the skill to a real task, and a verified competency milestone you can use to confirm you completed it. These steps reduce friction on future tasks and form a reliable baseline for every project you create.

Measure your setup by small, verifiable milestones. You have installed Unity Hub and logged in with a Unity ID when the Hub shows your account and offers Editor installs. You have installed an Editor with recommended modules when the Editor opens without missing build support warnings and Visual Studio launches for script editing. You’ve created a named 3D Core project when the Hub lists that project and opening it launches the Editor with a default scene. You can identify the five core Editor windows: Scene for constructing the world, Game for previewing camera output, Hierarchy for the scene’s GameObjects, Project for assets, and Inspector for component configuration. Finally, you can manipulate an object — add a Cube, use W/E/R hotkeys to Move/Rotate/Scale, change Transform values in the Inspector, and save the scene as MainScene. These are small, observable actions you can use to confirm competence and to avoid common mistakes like leaving assets unorganized or not saving your work.

Installing Unity Hub is the first practical step and it functions like mission control for your Unity installations. Unity Hub centralizes Editor versions and project management so you can install multiple Editor builds side-by-side. Begin by downloading the Hub installer from the provided source and follow the installer steps. When you first open Hub you'll be prompted to sign in with a Unity ID — creating one is a short, free process and it links your license and services. A common practical decision is to enable automatic updates or to pin an Editor version; for reproducibility, choose a stable recommended release or the Long Term Support version. After signing in, confirm Hub shows your account and offers the Editor installs page. A common misconception is that you must use the newest Editor right away; in many cases a stable LTS version reduces chance of breaking changes while you learn. Example: choose LTS if collaborating with teammates who use that version. Now consider build modules: include Visual Studio for scripting and your platform build support to prevent later build-time errors. This careful installation reduces interruptions when you begin scripting and building player targets.

After Hub is ready, you install a Unity Editor build and choose supporting modules. The Editor is the tool you will use to author scenes, attach scripts, and build players. When the Hub lists available Editor versions, consider the Long Term Support release because it prioritizes stability—useful when you move from tutorials to projects. During install, the Hub offers optional modules. For 3D development, include platform build support for your operating system and any target platforms you intend to test, such as Android or iOS, to avoid re-running the installer later. Also add Visual Studio Community so your code editing and debugging work smoothly. A concrete example: if you plan to test on Windows and Android, include Windows Build Support and Android Build Support during installation. A common misconception is that these modules can be skipped and added later without consequence; while you can add them later, doing so mid-project may interrupt your workflow and require a reinstall. Once installation completes, launch the Editor to verify that Visual Studio links and the Editor open without missing-module warnings. Install Editor and choose modules means install platform build support and visual studio during editor setup to enable building and scripting without later interruptions.. In practical terms, select an editor version and required modules for 3d development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating a new project is straightforward but important for long-term organization. In Unity Hub, click New Project and choose the 3D Core template. This template gives a clean starting scene with a camera and a directional light without unnecessary assets. Choose a meaningful project name such as MyFirst3DGame and select a dedicated location on your disk—preferably a Projects folder you keep for all Unity work. The folder location is critical: placing your project in a synced or shared folder can complicate locks and large asset syncing, so choose reliably accessible storage. When you click Create Project, Unity will open the Editor with the default layout and a new untitled scene. Immediately save the scene via File > Save Scene and name it MainScene. Saving early avoids losing work and establishes a predictable file structure. A common mistake is using cryptic or generic project names, which makes collaboration and version control harder. Naming and saving consistently is a small habit that pays off across a project’s lifetime. In practical terms, name, locate, and initialize your first scene. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Unity Editor is composed of a few interdependent windows you will use constantly. First, the Scene View is your interactive workspace where you place and arrange objects, adjust lighting, and visually build the game world. Think of it as a 3D canvas. The Game View renders what the active camera sees and helps you evaluate gameplay and framing. The Hierarchy shows a nested list of all GameObjects in the open scene; parenting affects transforms so a child moves with its parent. The Project window is your asset browser where models, scripts, textures, and audio live; keeping it tidy with descriptive folders prevents clutter. Finally, the Inspector exposes the properties and components of the currently selected GameObject or asset so you can edit Transform values, add components, or attach scripts. A common misconception is that the Hierarchy and Project windows list the same things — they do not. Hierarchy lists instances in the scene, Project lists source assets on disk. Example: importing a model appears in Project, and dragging it into the Scene creates a GameObject visible in Hierarchy. Understanding these roles makes navigation and editing efficient.

Scene navigation is a small set of controls that dramatically speed up level design once you practice them. The basic actions are pan, zoom, orbit, fly, and focus. Pan by holding the middle mouse button and dragging; this moves the Scene camera laterally. Zoom with the mouse scroll wheel to get closer to or farther from targets. Orbit by holding the right mouse button and dragging to rotate the camera around a pivot point; combine this with W, A, S, D to 'fly' through the scene while the right mouse button is held for first-person style movement. Use Q and E for vertical strafing. A highly useful shortcut is pressing F when an object is selected to focus the Scene camera on that object — the camera will center and zoom appropriately. A common novice mistake is confusing Scene and Game camera controls; Scene navigation affects your editing viewpoint only and does not change the game camera unless you edit that camera object. Example: select a cube and press F to immediately center it, then use W and right mouse to move closer while orbiting to inspect its surface. Practicing these controls makes placement and alignment much faster.

Adding GameObjects and manipulating their Transform component is one of the most frequent actions in Unity. To add your first object, right-click in the Hierarchy, choose 3D Object, and select Cube. The new Cube appears in the Scene View and as an entry in the Hierarchy. To move it, press W to activate the Move tool and drag the colored axes or use numeric values in the Transform component inside the Inspector. Press E for Rotate and R for Scale. A concrete example: place the Cube at position X:0, Y:1, Z:0 so it sits above the ground; rotate it 45 degrees on the Y axis to change its facing; scale it to 2 on the X axis to make it rectangular. A common beginner mistake is confusing which tool is active; if your object rotates when you intend to move it, switch to the Move tool with 'W'. Another tip is that you can type values directly into the Inspector for precise control. Practice both dragging handles and typing values so you can prototype quickly and then fine-tune numerically when precision is required.

Good project organization from the start saves hours later. The Project window is where assets live on disk and clutter builds up quickly if you leave everything at root. Adopt a simple folder structure such as Assets/Art, Assets/Scripts, Assets/Prefabs, Assets/Audio. Use descriptive file and folder names so assets are discoverable; for example, name a hero model Hero_V1 rather than model1. Importing a model places it into Project, and dragging it into the Scene creates an instance in the Hierarchy. A common rookie mistake is leaving many imported assets uncategorized, which slows you and your team. A practical habit is to create folders before importing and move new items into correct folders immediately. Also save scenes frequently with meaningful names like MainScene or Level01. Example: after importing a package, move textures into Art/Textures and meshes into Art/Models. This small organizational discipline reduces merge conflicts and makes searching faster when projects grow.
